note: Adjudicated variants: one of orthography (cenátum/cænátum, where both spellings are real words of the same recension and the edition rules which it prints), one of punctuation, and twenty-three of capitalization — twenty-two of them the words of consecration at w032-w053, the twenty-third the narrative Cálicem at w010 — twenty-five in all. Substantive text agrees across all three witnesses with zero further divergence.

adjudicated.ruling: Both spellings are real: ceno is the classical verb, and the ligature spellings cæno and cœno are the later ecclesiastical ones, all three headed by the dictionaries. The typical edition prints cenátum est in the Canon, and witness do follows it, so the edition prints that and records the hand missal's reading here rather than silently correcting a page that is not wrong. Whitaker's Words and Collatinus both head the classical spelling; Collatinus reads the ligature form under caeno.
The typical edition prints 'cálicem' where this edition prints 'Cálicem'; the reading is the same and only the case differs. Recorded rather than corrected.
Full stop closing the command to the disciples, with do and with the typical edition — parallel to the ruling at ordinarium.qui-pridie w038.

The words of consecration are set in the case the TYPICAL EDITION prints — Hoc est enim Corpus meum, Hic est enim Calix Sánguinis mei — with capitals only where that edition capitalises: the opening word, and Corpus, Calix and Sánguinis. Both hand missals set the whole formula in capitals, and this edition followed them until the typical edition itself could be read (leaf 386-387 of the 600 dpi scan, printed pages 306-307). The authority's own practice governs; the hand missals' capitals are recorded here rather than corrected, since neither page is wrong and the letters are identical.
